stories.title: You Love To See It: Keeping The Great Lakes Great
stories.text: Good things are happening! Michiganders blow up an oil pipeline, a state court puts a drugmaker under the microscope, Virginia settles scores with Jim Crow, and Illinois goes grocery shopping. You Love To See It is a benefit of a Lever paid subscription. Click Here To Upgrade Michigan’s One-Two Punch Against Big Oil Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, a scenic, rural region surrounded by three of North America’s five Great Lakes, is at the center of one of the most contentious issues in the state’s politics: an oil and gas pipeline called Enbridge Energy Line 5. The pipeline runs through both of Michigan’s peninsulas, but the Upper Peninsula has taken most of the damage from the million barrels of oil that have spilled out of the pipeline in its lifetime, all while hardly benefiting from the power it supplies. But when the Michigan Public Service Commission approved a tunnel project in 2023 to extend the pipeline’s lifespan, it didn’t consider evidence by environmentalists and Indigenous tribes that the project would be harmful to the environment. stories.title: Israel's Brutal Retaliation Against Imprisoned Palestinian Doctors Seeking Legal Appeals
stories.text: A Palestinian man walks past a portrait of imprisoned Kamal Adwan Hospital Director Dr. GAZA CITY—Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, the former director of the Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza, suffered multiple injuries, including fractured ribs, after enduring severe beatings by Israeli prison authorities on July 27, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Media Office. The group described it as the “most difficult day” of his imprisonment since being detained without charge over a year and a half ago. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the office said Abu Safiya, who suffers from heart disease and high blood pressure, has been subjected to “brutal torture” since June 24, when he was transferred to Rakevet—an underground detention facility within the Ramla prison complex in central Israel—including spending 21 days in solitary confinement. Previously, Abu Safiya told his lawyer, Nasser Odeh, during a prison visit on July 2, that following an appeal filed with the Israeli Supreme Court at the end of April, the assaults and abuse against him escalated dramatically.
